## S&P Historical Performance & Simulation

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(tidyquant)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

sp500 <- tq_get("^GSPC", 
from = "1950-01-01")
sp500

### Historical S&P 500 Index Level
### Index Level Over Time ### We're using the Return formula (Rt= (Pt/Pt-1)-1)
ggplot(data = sp500, aes(x = date, y = adjusted)) + geom_line()

### Historical Daily Returns
sp500 <- sp500 |> 
    mutate(
        daily_return = adjusted / lag(adjusted) -1 
    )
ggplot(data = sp500, aes(x = date, y = daily_return)) + geom_line()
    sp500

    annual_returns <- sp500 |> 
        tq_transmute(
            select = adjusted,
            mutate_fun = periodReturn,
            period = "yearly",
            type = "arithmetic"
        )
        annual_returns

        ### Annual Returns
        ggplot(
            data = annual_returns,
            aes(x = date, y = yearly.returns)
            ) + geom_col() + 
                scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
                labs(
                    title = "S&P 500 Annual Returns",
                    x = "Year",
                    y = "Annual Return"
                )

                ### Average Annnual Return, Median and Standard Deviation (Basically the volatility)

                mean(annual_returns$yearly.returns)
                median(annual_returns$yearly.returns)
                sd(annual_returns$yearly.returns)

### The distribution of annual returns

ggplot(
    data = annual_returns, 
    aes(x = yearly.returns)
)+ geom_histogram(bins = 30, color = "white") +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) + 
    labs(title = "Distribution of the S&P 500 Annual Returns",
    x = "Annual Return",
    y = "Number of Years")

### What percentage of years in our dataset had a negative S&P 500 return?
## Below is a smart way to calculate that using the mean and conditional
mean(annual_returns$yearly.returns < 0)

### Getting the actual number of negative years
annual_returns$yearly.returns < 0
sum(annual_returns$yearly.returns < 0)

### Calculating the Geometric Average Annual Return (Media Geometrica)
prod(1 + annual_returns$yearly.returns)^(1 / nrow(annual_returns)) - 1

### 9.61% is the arithmetic average of individual annual returns
### 8.29% is the constant compounded annual rate equivalent to the historical sequence in our dataset

### Mathematical Representation of Variation of Returns

return_stats <- annual_returns |> 
    summarize(
        mean_return = mean(yearly.returns),
        median_return = median(yearly.returns),
        sd_return = sd(yearly.returns),
        min_return = min(yearly.returns),
        max_returns = max(yearly.returns)
    )

    return_stats

### THE NORMAL DISTRIBUTION

rnorm(
    n=1,
    mean = return_stats$mean_return,
    sd = return_stats$sd_return
)
###If you want it in %
scales::percent(
    rnorm(
    n=1,
    mean = return_stats$mean_return,
    sd = return_stats$sd_return
)
)

### Going from one random year to a sequence of hypothetical future years.

simulated_returns <- rnorm(
    n=30,
    mean = return_stats$mean_return,
    sd = return_stats$sd_return
)
### a possible 30 year path.

###Investing $10k once. Results in 30 years.

initial_wealth <- 10000
wealth_path <- initial_wealth * cumprod(1 + simulated_returns)

wealth_path

simulation <- data.frame(year = 1:30,
rate = simulated_returns,
wealth = wealth_path)

simulation

ggplot(
    data = simulation,
    aes(x = year, y = wealth)) + 
        geom_line() + 
        labs(
            title = "One Simulated 30-Year Investment Path",
            x = "Year",
            y = "Portfolio Value"
        )

### Let's make it start from year 0 (10K)

simulation <- data.frame(
    year = 0:30,
    wealth = c(initial_wealth, wealth_path))

### Then run the same plot as before.

### Let's run 3 simulated paths

simulated_returns_3 <- matrix(
    rnorm(
        n = 30 * 3,
        mean = return_stats$mean_return,
        sd = return_stats$sd_return
    ),
    nrow = 30,
    ncol = 3
)

simulated_returns_3

### Converting those returns into wealth paths

wealth_paths_3 <- apply(
    simulated_returns_3,
    2,
    function(x) initial_wealth * cumprod(1 + x)
)
wealth_paths_3


### Visualizing these 3 simulations
simulation_3 <- data.frame(
    year = 0:30,
    path_1 = c(initial_wealth, wealth_paths_3[, 1]),
    path_2 = c(initial_wealth, wealth_paths_3[, 2]),
    path_3 = c(initial_wealth, wealth_paths_3[, 3])
)

simulation_3

ggplot(data = simulation_3,
aes(x = year)) + 
    geom_line(aes(y = path_1)) + 
    geom_line(aes(y = path_2)) +
    geom_line(aes(y = path_3)) + 
    labs(
        title = "Three Simulated 30-Year Investment Paths",
            x = "Year",
            y = "Portfolio Value",
    )

    ### Transforming the dataset from Wide format to Long format. 

    library(tidyr)
    simulation_3_long <- simulation_3 |>
        pivot_longer(
            cols = starts_with("path_"),
            names_to = "path",
            values_to = "wealth"
        )
        simulation_3_long

        ggplot(
            data = simulation_3_long,
            aes(
                x = year,
                y = wealth,
                group = path
            )
        ) +
            geom_line() +
            labs(
                title = "Three Simulated 30 Year Investment Paths",
                x = "Year",
                y = "Portfolio Value"
            )

### group = path connects observations belonging to the same path together. 

### MONTECARLO SIMULATION: 1000 POSSIBLE 30 YEAR FUTURES

n_years <- 30
n_simulations <- 1000

set.seed(123) ### if you rerun the code with seed 123 (or whatever number), you get the same sequence again.

simulated_returns_1000 <- matrix(
    rnorm(
        n = n_years * n_simulations,
        mean = return_stats$mean_return,
        sd = return_stats$sd_return
    ),
    nrow = n_years,
    ncol = n_simulations
)

dim(simulated_returns_1000)

### Compunding Formula to each column

wealth_paths_1000 <- apply(
    simulated_returns_1000,
    2,
    function(x) initial_wealth * cumprod(1 + x)
)
dim(wealth_paths_1000)

### Let's see the final row (where the investor ended up after the 30 years in each of the 1000 scenarios)

ending_wealth <- wealth_paths_1000[n_years, ]  ### We had set up n_years = 30. So row 30.
ending_wealth

length(ending_wealth)

summary(ending_wealth)

ending_wealth_df <- data.frame(
    wealth = ending_wealth
)

ggplot(
    data = ending_wealth_df,
    aes(x = wealth)
) +
    geom_histogram() +
    labs(
        title = "Distribution of Ending Wealth After 30 Years",
        x = "Ending Portfolio Value",
        y = "Number of Simulations"
    )

    ### Percentiles
    quantile(
        ending_wealth,
        probs = c(0.10, 0.50, 0.90)
    )

median_path <- apply(
    wealth_paths_1000,
    1,
    median
)    
median_path

lower_path <- apply(
    wealth_paths_1000,
    1,
    quantile,
    probs = 0.90
)
lower_path

upper_path <- apply(
    wealth_paths_1000,
    1,
    quantile,
    probs = 0.10
)
upper_path

### Putting median_path, lower_path and upper_path in one data frame

percentile_paths <- data.frame(
    year = 1:n_years,
    lower = lower_path,
    median = median_path,
    upper = upper_path
)

percentile_paths

###

ggplot(
    data = percentile_paths,
    aes(x = year)
) +
    geom_ribbon(
        aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper),
        alpha = 0.3
    ) + 
        geom_line(
            aes(y = median)
        ) + 
            labs(
                title = "Montecarlo Simulation of Portfolio Wealth",
                x = "Year",
                y = "Portfolio Value"
            )
```
